title: Downward self-reducibility of integer factoring
formal: Is there one deterministic oracle Turing machine A and a polynomial p such that, for every integer \(N\ge 2\) of binary length n, A outputs the complete prime factorization of N within \(p(n)\) steps, using a factoring oracle only on integers \(M\ge 2\) whose binary length is strictly less than n?

source_formulation.text: It is an open problem whether there exists an algorithm for factoring that uses oracle calls on smaller numbers.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 15

context:
Downward self-reducibility asks whether oracle solutions to strictly shorter instances suffice to solve the current instance with only polynomial additional work.

Definition 2.17 compares binary input lengths. The source separately defines a circuit-based notion, which is not substituted here. The retained card makes the shorter-input convention explicit.

The source shows that downward self-reducibility of factoring would place it in UEOPL, linking arithmetic factorization with a unique structured total-search class. This consequence does not decide whether the reduction exists.

sentences: Factoring is a central arithmetic search problem whose complete output is a unique prime-power decomposition.
The question asks whether one can factor an n-bit number in polynomial time given oracle answers only on shorter numbers.
All queries must have fewer than n bits, not merely a smaller numerical value.
The reducer is deterministic and uniform, with polynomially many ordinary computation steps.
A positive answer would place factoring in a more structured total-search class and reveal a basic recursive property of the problem.

definitions: The input is the ordinary base-two expansion of N without leading zeroes, and \(n=\lfloor \log _{2}N\rfloor +1\). The output is the list of distinct increasing primes \(q_{1}<\cdots <q_{r}\) and positive integer exponents \(e_{i}\), all in binary, with \(N=\prod _{i} q_{i}^{e_{i}}\). A prime input has the single pair \((N,1)\). The oracle returns the same unique prime-factorization representation on M. Queries may be adaptive but must all satisfy \(\lfloor \log _{2}M\rfloor +1<n\) relative to the original input length. Merely requiring \(M<N\) would be weaker and is not the target. The ordinary Turing-machine cost includes writing queries, reading answers and writing the output; supplying a correct oracle answer is the sole oracle operation. The output length of prime factorization is polynomial in n. There is no randomness, advice or nonuniform family of reducers. The reduction must work for every input, with one polynomial bound independent of its factorization.
answer_criterion: Prove existence of the uniform polynomial-time reduction or its logical negation. Factoring using smaller numerical values of the same bit length, arbitrary smaller circuits for a factoring relation, or an exponential-time recursion does not meet the stated definition. The output need not be a decimal expansion of the input; its prime-power representation is explicit.
